function.name: generate_sea_foam
function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The “color” you see when looking out over the ocean isn’t fixed—it’s a mix of physics, biology, and geography all playing together: | Factor | How it changes what we see | |--------|-----------------------------| | **Depth** | In shallow waters (< 5 m), sunlight penetrates fully so the water looks more *green* because chlorophyll‑rich algae absorb red light and reflect green/blue wavelengths. Deeper down (> 30–50 m) only short‑wavelength blue light reaches us; everything else gets absorbed, giving a deep *azure* or even *navy* hue. | | **Angle & Sun Position** | At sunrise/sunset the sun shines through longer paths of air and water, scattering shorter wavelengths away and leaving reds/oranges—so the sea may look pinkish or golden. Midday overhead sun gives a bright, clear blue. | | **Water Composition** | • **Phytoplankton blooms** → greener tint.
• **Suspended sediments / runoff** → murkier, brownish or grayish tones.
• **Salt content** doesn’t directly change color, but higher salinity slightly increases refractive index, making reflections sharper. | | **Surface Conditions** | Calm seas show a crisp, almost mirror‑like blue. Rough surf breaks up light into many angles, creating frothy whites and a washed‑out appearance. | | **Geographic Location** | Tropical reefs often appear vivid turquoise because coral skeletons scatter light strongly. Arctic ice fronts give a pale cyan or icy blue. Near coasts with sandy bottoms, reflected sand can add yellow/gold undertones. | So while most people think of the sea as “deep blue,” its actual shade ranges from emerald greens off tropical shores, to azure blues in open oceans, to muddy browns where rivers meet the sea, and even to sparkling white foamy caps during storms.
